courses.title: Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery
courses.description: Local anaesthesia, exodontia and minor oral surgery, maxillofacial trauma, infections, cleft lip and palate, TMJ disorders and medical emergencies in the dental chair.

topics.title: Local Anaesthesia in Dentistry
topics.summary: Agents, techniques (inferior alveolar nerve block, infiltration), doses and complications.

material.heading: Agents and techniques
material.body: Common dental local anaesthetics: lidocaine 2% with 1:80,000 or 1:100,000 adrenaline (maximum about 4.4–7 mg/kg with adrenaline; one 2.2 mL cartridge contains 44 mg), articaine 4% with adrenaline (good infiltration penetration — effective buccal infiltration even for lower molars), mepivacaine and prilocaine with felypressin (useful where adrenaline is to be avoided). Techniques: infiltration (maxillary teeth — thin porous bone; mandibular anterior teeth), inferior alveolar nerve block (IANB — for mandibular molars and premolars; needle inserted at the pterygomandibular space medial to the coronoid notch at the level of the occlusal plane, anaesthetising the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves; long buccal nerve block for buccal soft tissues), mental and incisive blocks, and intraligamentary injections. Always aspirate to avoid intravascular injection. Paediatric doses must be calculated by weight.

material.heading: Complications
material.body: Local complications: failure of anaesthesia (anatomical variation, infection — low pH reduces effectiveness), haematoma, trismus (medial pterygoid injury), transient facial nerve palsy (injection into the parotid capsule during IANB — protect the eye), prolonged paraesthesia (lingual/inferior alveolar nerves — more with 4% solutions in blocks), self-inflicted soft-tissue biting in children (warn parents), needle breakage and infection. Systemic complications: fainting (vasovagal syncope — the most common medical emergency in dentistry; lie the patient flat with legs raised), toxicity (overdose or intravascular injection — CNS then cardiovascular effects), allergy (rare with amides; often to preservatives or latex), adrenaline effects (palpitations, anxiety), and methaemoglobinaemia (prilocaine, articaine at high doses). Patients with cardiac disease can generally receive adrenaline-containing LA in limited doses.

topics.title: Exodontia and Minor Oral Surgery
topics.summary: Extraction principles, complications, surgical removal of third molars and post-extraction care.

material.heading: Extractions
material.body: Assess medical history (anticoagulants — check INR within 24–72 hours, extract if INR < 4 with local haemostasis; antiplatelets usually continued; bisphosphonates; radiotherapy; bleeding disorders; diabetes; cardiac conditions; pregnancy). Forceps extraction uses controlled luxation and expansion of the socket; elevators (Coupland's, Warwick James, Cryer's) luxate and remove roots. Post-extraction instructions: bite on gauze for 20–30 minutes, avoid rinsing and hot drinks for 24 hours, then warm salt-water rinses, avoid smoking. Complications: haemorrhage (primary, reactionary within 24 hours, secondary after 7–10 days from infection — pressure, local haemostatic agents (oxidised cellulose, sutures, tranexamic acid mouthwash)), dry socket (alveolar osteitis — severe pain on day 2–4 with an empty socket and halitosis, more common in smokers, lower molars and women on oral contraceptives; irrigate and dress with Alvogyl; analgesics — antibiotics not needed), fracture of tooth or tuberosity, oroantral communication (upper molars/premolars — if small, heals; larger — buccal advancement flap; advise no nose blowing), displacement of roots into the antrum or tissue spaces, and damage to adjacent teeth.
keyPoints: Bite on gauze; no rinsing 24 h

material.heading: Third molars and minor surgery
material.body: Impacted lower third molars are classified by angulation (mesioangular — commonest and easiest; vertical; horizontal; distoangular — most difficult) and depth relative to the occlusal plane and ramus (Pell and Gregory). Indications for removal: recurrent pericoronitis, unrestorable caries, periodontal disease affecting the second molar, cysts or tumours, and resorption of adjacent teeth; prophylactic removal of asymptomatic teeth is not routinely recommended. Radiographic signs of close relationship to the inferior alveolar canal (darkening of the root, interruption of the white lines, diversion of the canal) warrant CBCT or coronectomy. Surgical removal: flap design, bone removal, tooth sectioning, debridement and suturing; complications — pain, swelling, trismus, dry socket, and nerve injury (inferior alveolar — lower lip numbness; lingual — tongue numbness). Pericoronitis (inflammation of the operculum over a partially erupted tooth): irrigation, warm saline rinses, analgesics, and metronidazole if systemic signs. Other minor oral surgery: biopsies, apicectomy, frenectomy, and exposure of impacted canines for orthodontics.

topics.title: Maxillofacial Trauma
topics.summary: Assessment, mandibular and midface fractures, dental trauma and management principles.

material.heading: Assessment and mandible
material.body: Maxillofacial injuries in Nigeria mostly result from road traffic crashes (motorcycles — okada), assaults, falls and gunshots. Primary survey (airway — tongue falling back in bilateral mandibular fractures, blood, teeth, dentures; cervical spine protection; bleeding) takes priority, then assess for head injury. Mandibular fractures are the commonest facial fractures; sites: condyle (most common in many series), angle, body, parasymphysis. Signs: pain, swelling, deranged occlusion, step deformity, sublingual haematoma (pathognomonic of mandibular fracture), paraesthesia of the lower lip (inferior alveolar nerve), and trismus. Imaging: OPG and PA mandible or CT. Management: closed reduction with intermaxillary fixation (arch bars, eyelet wires — for 4–6 weeks; wire cutters must be kept with the patient) or open reduction and internal fixation with miniplates (Champy's lines) allowing early function. Antibiotics for fractures through tooth-bearing areas (compound into the mouth).

material.heading: Midface and dental trauma
material.body: Le Fort fractures of the maxilla: Le Fort I (horizontal, above the teeth — mobile tooth-bearing segment), Le Fort II (pyramidal — through the nasal bones, infraorbital margins), Le Fort III (craniofacial dysjunction — through the zygomatic arches and orbits; 'dish face', CSF rhinorrhoea, periorbital oedema). Zygomatic complex fractures: flattening of the cheek, periorbital ecchymosis, subconjunctival haemorrhage with no posterior limit, infraorbital nerve paraesthesia, trismus (coronoid impingement) and diplopia; orbital floor ('blow-out') fractures cause enophthalmos and restricted upward gaze (inferior rectus entrapment). Retrobulbar haemorrhage (pain, proptosis, falling vision) is an emergency (lateral canthotomy). Dental trauma: fractures of enamel, dentine or pulp; luxation injuries; avulsion — replant an avulsed permanent tooth immediately (hold by the crown, rinse briefly, reinsert, or store in milk/saliva; splint for about 2 weeks); do not replant primary teeth. Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics as indicated.
keyPoints: Le Fort III: dish face, CSF leak
Replant avulsed permanent tooth; store in milk

topics.title: Cleft Lip and Palate and TMJ Disorders
topics.summary: Cleft classification and multidisciplinary care, and temporomandibular joint disorders.

material.heading: Cleft lip and palate
material.body: Orofacial clefts are among the commonest congenital anomalies (about 1 in 1,000 births in Nigeria; cleft lip with or without palate more common in boys; isolated cleft palate more in girls). Causes: multifactorial — genetics, maternal smoking, alcohol, anticonvulsants, folic acid deficiency; some syndromic (Pierre Robin sequence — micrognathia, glossoptosis, airway obstruction). Problems: feeding (special bottles, squeezable, positioning upright), speech (hypernasality, velopharyngeal insufficiency), hearing (otitis media with effusion), dental anomalies, appearance and psychosocial stigma. Multidisciplinary team management: lip repair at about 3 months (rule of 10s — 10 weeks, 10 lb, Hb 10 g/dL), palate repair at 6–12 months (before speech develops), alveolar bone grafting at 8–11 years (before canine eruption), orthodontics, speech therapy, ENT and possible orthognathic surgery. Smile Train and other programmes have supported free cleft surgery across Nigeria.

material.heading: Temporomandibular disorders
material.body: Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) are common: myofascial pain (masticatory muscle pain, often related to stress and parafunction — bruxism, clenching), disc displacement (with reduction — clicking; without reduction — closed lock, limited opening), and degenerative joint disease (crepitus). Management is mainly conservative: reassurance, soft diet, jaw rest, heat, analgesics (NSAIDs), physiotherapy and jaw exercises, occlusal splints, stress management and low-dose amitriptyline for chronic pain; arthrocentesis or surgery rarely. TMJ ankylosis (bony or fibrous fusion — commonly after trauma (condylar fractures) or infection in childhood, including after noma; limited mouth opening, facial asymmetry, micrognathia, airway problems) requires surgical release (gap arthroplasty, interpositional grafts, costochondral grafts) with aggressive postoperative physiotherapy. TMJ dislocation (anterior — mouth locked open after yawning; reduced by downward and backward pressure on the molars).

topics.title: Medical Emergencies and Special Care in Oral Surgery
topics.summary: Emergency drugs and management in the dental setting, and care of medically compromised patients.

material.heading: Medical emergencies
material.body: Every dental clinic needs trained staff, oxygen, a bag–valve–mask, suction, an AED, and emergency drugs: adrenaline 1:1000 (IM 0.5 mg for adult anaphylaxis), aspirin 300 mg (chest pain), glyceryl trinitrate spray (angina), salbutamol inhaler (asthma), glucose gel/oral glucose and glucagon (hypoglycaemia), and midazolam (buccal — prolonged seizures). Emergencies: vasovagal syncope (lie flat, raise legs), hypoglycaemia (oral glucose if conscious; glucagon IM if not), asthma (salbutamol via spacer; oxygen; call for help if severe), anaphylaxis (IM adrenaline, oxygen, call emergency services, repeat after 5 minutes), angina/myocardial infarction (GTN, aspirin, oxygen if hypoxic), epileptic seizure (protect from injury, midazolam if > 5 minutes), choking/inhalation of instruments (back blows and abdominal thrusts; rubber dam prevents), adrenal crisis, and cardiac arrest (CPR 30:2, AED). The ABCDE approach structures assessment.

material.heading: Medically compromised patients
material.body: Bleeding risk: anticoagulants (warfarin — INR; DOACs — often timing extractions before the next dose), antiplatelets (usually continued), haemophilia (factor replacement with haematologist; tranexamic acid) and liver disease. Infective endocarditis: antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk patients (previous endocarditis, prosthetic valves, certain congenital heart disease) per current guidelines; good oral health is more important. Diabetes: schedule morning appointments, ensure the patient has eaten and taken medication, and manage infections aggressively. Hypertension: defer elective treatment if BP ≥ 180/110. Pregnancy: second trimester is best for elective treatment; avoid unnecessary radiographs; lidocaine is safe. HIV: standard precautions; manage oral lesions; no special restrictions for routine care. Bisphosphonates/antiresorptives: risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) — dental assessment before starting, atraumatic extractions. Radiotherapy: osteoradionecrosis risk — pre-radiotherapy extractions. Sickle cell disease: avoid prolonged procedures, dehydration and infection; consider prophylaxis.
